listeningParts.title: Booking a ferry and a holiday cottage
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones an island ferry and accommodation office to arrange a short holiday.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, Inishkerrow Ferries and Island Holidays, Declan speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. My partner and I are planning a few days on Inishkerrow this summer, and I'd like to book the ferry and somewhere to stay, if that's possible.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: No problem at all, we can do both. Are you bringing a car, or travelling as foot passengers?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We were thinking of bringing the car. Is that a good idea?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: To be honest, the island's only about six kilometres long, and most people walk or cycle. But you can bring a car on the larger ferry. The vehicle has to be under five metres long, though, because the deck is quite small.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Ours is a small hatchback, so that's fine. How long is the crossing?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: On the car ferry it's forty-five minutes. There's also a fast passenger boat that takes about twenty-five minutes, but it doesn't carry vehicles.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We'll take the car ferry. What are the fares?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: A single ticket is fourteen euros per adult, and a return is twenty-four euros. The car is an extra thirty-five euros return, and that includes the driver's ticket, so you'd pay for one adult return plus the car.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: So fifty-nine euros altogether. That sounds fine. And the accommodation?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: We manage four self-catering cottages on the island. When would you like to come?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We were hoping to arrive on the twelfth of July and stay four nights.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Let me check. Ah, the cottages are all booked on the twelfth, I'm afraid, because there's a music festival on the island that weekend. But I could offer you the fourteenth to the eighteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The fourteenth works. We're flexible.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Great. The cottage that's free then is called Seal Cottage. It's right beside the old harbour, and you can often see seals on the rocks from the kitchen window. It has one double bedroom, a small garden, and a wood-burning stove in the sitting room, which is lovely in the evenings, even in July.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds perfect. How much is it?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's ninety-five euros a night, so three hundred and eighty for the four nights. Bed linen and towels are included, and there's a basket of firewood for the stove.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And what about food? Is there a supermarket?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: There's one small shop near the pier, which sells most basics, as well as fresh fish and bread from the island bakery. It's open every day except Wednesday afternoons, when it closes at one. But I'd recommend bringing some supplies with you, as prices are a bit higher than on the mainland.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Good to know. Can we pay by card on the island?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: The shop and the café take cards, but there's no bank and no cash machine on the island, and a few places, like the bike hire, only accept cash. So it's worth bringing some euros with you.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Where's the bike hire?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's run from the café, just up the hill from the pier. Bikes are twelve euros a day. Honestly, if you're hiring bikes, you might want to leave your car on the mainland and save the money.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hmm, you might be right. Let me talk to my partner about that. Can I book the cottage now and the ferry later?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. I'll just need your name for the booking.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Joanna Pruett. That's P-R-U-E-T-T.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you. And a phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My cell number is oh-one-five-five, three-two-nine, eight-four-one.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. We ask for a deposit of one hundred euros to hold the cottage, and the rest is due two weeks before you arrive. I'll email you the payment details today.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. Is there anything else we should bring?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Definitely a good waterproof jacket. The weather out here can change very quickly, even in summer. And if you're walking to the cliffs at the north end, wear proper boots, because the path can be muddy.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Thanks so much, Declan. You've been really helpful.

listeningParts.title: Welcome to Holm Island nature reserve
listeningParts.contextDescription: A ranger speaks to a group of day visitors as they arrive by boat at an island nature reserve.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Holm Island. My name's Ben, and I'm one of the two rangers who live here from March to October. Before you set off, I'd like to give you some information about the island and a few rules, so that you have a good day and the wildlife isn't disturbed.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Holm Island has been a nature reserve since 1976. Before that, there was a small farming community here, but the last family left in the 1950s, mainly because the children had to go to the mainland for secondary school and the parents didn't want to be separated from them. Since then, the island has belonged entirely to the birds and the seals, and to visitors like you, of course.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Most people come here to see the seabirds, and you've chosen a very good time. In June the colonies are at their busiest. We have around twelve thousand pairs of puffins, which nest in burrows in the grassy slopes above the cliffs. The burrows are only a short distance under the surface, and the ground is easily broken, so it's extremely important that you stay on the marked paths. If you step off the path, you could collapse a burrow with a chick inside.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: You'll also see razorbills, guillemots and kittiwakes on the cliff ledges. A lot of visitors ask whether the numbers are going up or down. The honest answer is that puffins here are fairly stable at the moment, but kittiwakes have declined by about a third in the last twenty years. The main cause seems to be changes in the sea, which mean there are fewer of the small fish they feed their chicks on.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: A few rules. There are no bins on the island, so please take all your rubbish back with you on the boat. Dogs aren't allowed, as you probably saw on the booking website. And please don't feed the gulls, however friendly they look. They've learned that visitors carry sandwiches, and they can be quite bold.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: The boat leaves again at four o'clock, and it won't wait, so please be back at the landing stage by a quarter to four. If you miss it, you'll be spending the night with me, and I can promise you the accommodation isn't very comfortable.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: Now, let me tell you about the main places to visit. If you look at the map on the board here, you'll see the landing stage at the bottom, and the visitor hut just above it. The hut has toilets, which are the only ones on the island, and an exhibition about the island's history, including photographs of the families who once lived here.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: If you follow the main path north for about twenty minutes, you'll reach the North Cliffs. This is the best place to see puffins close up. In fact, they often walk right up to the path. There's a wooden screen with viewing holes, so you can watch them without disturbing them.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: On the west side of the island is Seal Bay. Grey seals rest on the rocks there at low tide, and today low tide is at about one o'clock, so that's the best time to go. Please keep your voices down, because the seals are easily frightened and will go into the water if they hear people.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: In the middle of the island, you'll find the old walled garden, which belonged to the farm. It's sheltered from the wind, so it's a good spot for a picnic, and there are benches there. It's also where we've planted wild flowers that attract butterflies and bees.

dialogue.speaker: Ranger
dialogue.text: And finally, at the southern tip, there's the lighthouse. It's been automatic since the 1980s, so there are no keepers any more, and you can't go inside. But on Wednesdays and Saturdays, I give a short talk there at two o'clock about the history of the lighthouse, which you're welcome to join. Right, enjoy your day.

listeningParts.title: A project on island depopulation
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two geography students, Ella and Tom, discuss their research on population decline in small islands with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Ella, Tom, come and sit down. So, how's the island project going?

dialogue.speaker: Ella
dialogue.text: Really well, thanks. As you know, we're looking at why the populations of small islands off the coasts of Scotland and Ireland have fallen, and whether anything can reverse it. We've now finished our background reading and started on the case studies.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. What did you find in the reading?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The general pattern is quite clear. Most of these islands reached their highest population in the nineteenth century, and since then numbers have dropped, sometimes very steeply. The most famous extreme case is St Kilda, where the last thirty-six inhabitants asked to be taken to the mainland in 1930, and the island has had no permanent population since then.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what are the main reasons for decline, generally?

dialogue.speaker: Ella
dialogue.text: Lack of jobs is always mentioned first. Traditional work like fishing and small-scale farming doesn't support as many people as it used to. But what surprised me was how often education came up. On a lot of islands, once the primary school closes, families with young children leave, and then it's very hard to get them back.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: It becomes a kind of cycle. Fewer children means the school closes, and without a school, younger families won't move there, so the population gets older and older.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a good point to develop. Have you found any examples of islands where the trend has been reversed?

dialogue.speaker: Ella
dialogue.text: Yes, a few. The best examples seem to be places where the community itself bought the land. In Scotland, there have been several community buyouts, where residents raised money to buy the island from a private landowner. Afterwards, they were able to build affordable housing and attract new families.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The other big change is broadband. Since fast internet reached some islands, a few people have moved there to work remotely for companies on the mainland, or even abroad. One woman we interviewed runs a graphic design business from her kitchen.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So you've done interviews as well?

dialogue.speaker: Ella
dialogue.text: Yes, by video call. We spoke to fourteen people on three islands. We'd hoped to visit one of them, but the ferry was cancelled twice because of storms, so in the end we had to do everything online.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a shame, but it's actually a nice illustration of your topic. Transport problems are part of island life. Did the interviews tell you anything you didn't expect?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The thing that came up most often wasn't jobs or schools, actually. It was housing. Several people said that holiday homes were pushing up prices, so that young islanders couldn't afford to stay, even when they had work.

dialogue.speaker: Ella
dialogue.text: And one man said that some houses are empty for ten months of the year, which makes the villages feel deserted in winter.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important tension, because tourism also brings income. You'll need to present both sides. Now, how are you going to structure the final report?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We thought we'd start with the historical background, then the three case studies, and finish with recommendations.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'd suggest putting a short section comparing the three islands before the recommendations. That way, the reader can see the patterns clearly. And please include a table with the population figures for each island at each census, so the trends are easy to see.

dialogue.speaker: Ella
dialogue.text: Okay, that makes sense. Should we include quotes from the interviews?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Definitely, but keep them short, and make sure you've got permission from everyone you quote. Some of these communities are very small, so even without names, people might be recognised. You could ask them to check the quotes before you submit.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Good idea. When do you need the draft?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: By the end of next month, please. And send me the interview questions too, so I can include them in the appendix check.

listeningParts.title: The theory of island biogeography
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an ecology course about why some islands have more species than others.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today we're going to look at one of the most influential ideas in ecology, which tries to answer a simple question: why do some islands have many more species than others?

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Naturalists had noticed for a long time that large islands generally support more species than small ones. If you count the species of birds, reptiles or plants on a group of islands, and plot them against the area of each island, you get a fairly regular pattern. This is known as the species-area relationship. As a rough rule, an island ten times larger than another will have about twice as many species.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: But it wasn't until the 1960s that two American ecologists, Robert MacArthur and Edward Wilson, offered a full explanation. In 1967 they published a book called The Theory of Island Biogeography, and their central idea was that the number of species on an island reflects a balance between two processes: immigration and extinction.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's take immigration first. New species arrive on islands all the time: birds and bats fly there, seeds are carried by the wind or by birds, and insects and small reptiles may float across the sea on pieces of vegetation. MacArthur and Wilson pointed out that the rate of arrival depends mainly on distance. An island close to the mainland will receive new arrivals much more often than a remote one in the middle of the ocean.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now extinction. Once a species arrives, it may not survive. On a small island, populations are small, and small populations are much more likely to die out, for example after a storm, a drought or a disease. So the rate of extinction depends mainly on the size of the island. Over time, the two rates come into balance, and the number of species stays roughly constant, even though the actual species present may keep changing. They called this an equilibrium.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The theory makes two clear predictions. Large islands close to the mainland should have the most species, and small, remote islands the fewest. And these predictions have generally been supported by the evidence.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Wilson also tested the theory directly, together with his student Daniel Simberloff. In the late 1960s, they chose several tiny mangrove islands off the coast of Florida, each only a few metres across, and covered them with tents before removing all the insects and spiders with chemicals. Then they watched as the islands were recolonised. Within about a year, the number of species on each island had returned to roughly its original level, and, as the theory predicted, the nearest islands recovered fastest, although the species were not all the same as before.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Nature has also provided its own experiments. When the volcano Krakatoa in Indonesia erupted in 1883, it destroyed all life on the remaining islands. Scientists who visited in the following decades recorded the return of plants and animals, starting with ferns and grasses. And in 1963, a completely new island, called Surtsey, appeared in the sea off the south coast of Iceland after a volcanic eruption. It was immediately protected, and only scientists are allowed to land, so that they can study how life arrives. The first plant was recorded there in 1965, just two years after the island appeared.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What makes the theory so important today, though, is that it doesn't only apply to real islands. Think of a forest that has been cut into small patches by farmland or roads. Each patch is effectively an island surrounded by an environment that many forest species can't cross. The same is true of many national parks. So the theory helps to explain why species disappear when habitats are fragmented, and it has influenced the design of nature reserves. For example, it suggests that one large reserve may often be better than several small ones, and that corridors of habitat connecting reserves can help species to move between them.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: That said, the theory has its limitations. It treats all species as if they were equal, and it pays little attention to the evolution of new species on islands, which is particularly important on very remote islands such as Hawaii. We'll come back to that next week, when we look at island evolution.

readingPassages.title: The statues of Rapa Nui
paragraphs: Rapa Nui, also known as Easter Island, is one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth. A triangle of volcanic rock covering only about 164 square kilometres, it lies in the south-eastern Pacific Ocean, more than three thousand five hundred kilometres west of the coast of Chile, to which it belongs. The nearest inhabited island, Pitcairn, is around two thousand kilometres away. Yet this tiny, isolated island is famous throughout the world for the giant stone statues, known as moai, that were carved by its Polynesian inhabitants centuries ago.

The island's first settlers were Polynesian seafarers, who reached it by canoe after a remarkable voyage across open ocean. Exactly when they arrived is still debated. Earlier researchers suggested a date in the first millennium AD, but more recent radiocarbon dating has led many archaeologists to conclude that settlement took place around 1200. The settlers brought with them crops such as sweet potato and taro, as well as chickens. They also brought, probably by accident, the Polynesian rat, an animal that would have important consequences for the island's environment.

Nearly a thousand moai have been recorded on the island. Most are between three and six metres tall, but the largest ever raised, known as Paro, is around ten metres high and is estimated to weigh more than eighty tonnes. Almost all of them were carved from a soft volcanic rock called tuff, at a quarry in the crater of an extinct volcano, Rano Raraku. Hundreds of statues remain at the quarry today, some still attached to the rock in which they were being carved, which gives archaeologists a valuable picture of how the work was done, using hard stone tools.

Once finished, many moai were transported to stone platforms, called ahu, near the coast. Most of these statues face inland, towards the villages, rather than out to sea, and it is widely believed that they represented important ancestors who watched over the community. Some were given red stone 'hats', called pukao, made from a different type of volcanic rock from another quarry. How the islanders moved such heavy objects across the island, sometimes for more than ten kilometres, has been one of the great puzzles of Pacific archaeology.

For many years, the most popular theory was that the statues were laid on wooden sledges and dragged, which would have required large quantities of timber. This idea fitted a well-known account of the island's history, popularised by the geographer Jared Diamond in his 2005 book Collapse. According to this view, the islanders cut down their forests to move statues and clear land, which led to soil erosion, food shortages and conflict, and a dramatic fall in population. The island became a warning about what happens when a society destroys its own environment.

In recent years, however, this story has been strongly challenged. The archaeologists Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo have argued that the rats introduced by the first settlers, which ate the seeds of the island's palm trees, played a major part in the loss of the forest. They have also suggested that the moai were 'walked' upright, rocked from side to side by teams pulling on ropes. In 2012, they demonstrated this method with a replica statue weighing several tonnes, which a team of fewer than twenty people moved along a road with surprising speed. This method would have required far less wood than dragging.

What is not disputed is that the greatest disaster in the island's history came from outside. Europeans first reached Rapa Nui on Easter Sunday in 1722, when the Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen arrived and gave the island its European name. In the 1860s, raiders from Peru took around fifteen hundred islanders away to work as slaves, and diseases such as smallpox, brought back by a few survivors who were returned, spread rapidly. By 1877, only around one hundred and eleven Rapa Nui people remained on the island.

Today the population is several thousand, and the island's culture is experiencing a revival. Rapa Nui National Park was added to the World Heritage List in 1995, and tourism is now the main source of income. Many islanders have campaigned for the return of statues taken abroad, including one called Hoa Hakananai'a, which has been in the British Museum in London since 1869. For the Rapa Nui people, the moai are not simply archaeological objects, but living links with their ancestors.

readingPassages.title: Giants and dwarfs: the strange evolution of island animals
paragraphs: Islands have long fascinated biologists, and for good reason. Cut off from the mainland, often for millions of years, island plants and animals evolve in isolation, and the results can be remarkable. Charles Darwin's visit to the Galápagos Islands in 1835 helped to shape his ideas about evolution, and islands continue to serve as natural laboratories. One of the most striking patterns they reveal concerns body size: on islands, small animals often become larger, while large animals often become smaller.

This pattern was first described systematically by the Canadian biologist J. Bristol Foster, who published a study of island mammals in the journal Nature in 1964. Foster compared mammals living on islands off the west coast of North America with their relatives on the mainland, and noticed that island rodents tended to be larger, while island deer and carnivores tended to be smaller. Nine years later, the American biologist Leigh Van Valen gave the pattern a name, the island rule, and it has been debated by scientists ever since.

The fossil record provides some dramatic examples of dwarfing. During the last ice ages, elephants reached several islands in the Mediterranean Sea, including Sicily, Malta and Cyprus, probably by swimming, as modern elephants are strong swimmers. Over many generations, their descendants shrank. Some of the dwarf elephants of Sicily and Malta stood barely a metre tall at the shoulder, compared with their mainland ancestors, which were among the largest elephants that ever lived. On Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean, a population of woolly mammoths survived until around four thousand years ago, long after mammoths had disappeared from the mainland.

Even humans may not have been an exception. In 2003, archaeologists working in a cave on the Indonesian island of Flores discovered the remains of a previously unknown human species, which they named Homo floresiensis. Adults appear to have been only around a metre tall, and the species was quickly nicknamed 'the hobbit'. Some researchers have suggested that its small size is another example of island dwarfing, although its origins are still the subject of intense debate.

At the other end of the scale, some islands have produced giants. The Komodo dragon of Indonesia, the world's largest living lizard, can grow to around three metres long. The Galápagos Islands and Aldabra in the Indian Ocean are home to giant tortoises, and on Mauritius lived the dodo, a large flightless relative of pigeons. New Zealand, which had no land mammals apart from bats before humans arrived, was once home to the moa, enormous flightless birds, the largest of which could reach a height of more than three metres with its neck stretched upwards.

Why should islands produce these opposite effects? The most common explanation is that islands offer a very different set of challenges from the mainland. Large animals need a great deal of food, and on a small island, resources are limited, so smaller individuals, which need less food, may be more likely to survive and reproduce. Small animals, on the other hand, are often freed from the predators that kept them small and hidden on the mainland, and from competition with other species, which allows them to grow larger. In the absence of predators, many island birds also lost the ability to fly, as flight requires a great deal of energy.

Unfortunately, the same features that allowed island animals to flourish in isolation also made them extremely vulnerable when humans arrived. Animals that had never encountered predators were often unafraid of people, and flightless birds could not escape. The dodo was first described by Dutch sailors in 1598, and within less than a century it had disappeared, hunted by sailors and attacked by the rats, pigs and other animals they brought with them. In New Zealand, all species of moa were hunted to extinction within a few centuries of the arrival of the first Polynesian settlers.

Not all scientists are convinced that the island rule is a true rule. Some studies have found many exceptions, and in 2008, a group of researchers led by Shai Meiri argued that the pattern was much weaker than had been assumed for many groups of mammals. Others have pointed out that the size of an island, its distance from the mainland and its climate all seem to influence the result. However, more recent large-scale analyses, comparing hundreds of island species with their mainland relatives, have found that the general trend does exist across mammals, birds and reptiles, even if it is far from universal.

readingPassages.title: Can the atoll nations survive?
paragraphs: Scattered across the Pacific and Indian Oceans are a handful of countries made up almost entirely of coral atolls: rings of low, narrow islands built from sand and broken coral on top of ancient reefs. Kiribati, Tuvalu, the Marshall Islands and the Maldives are among them. Most of their land lies only a few metres above sea level, and in the case of the Maldives, the great majority is less than a metre above the sea. As global sea levels rise, these nations face a threat that no other country has experienced: the possibility that their entire territory could become uninhabitable.

The dangers are not only a matter of slow flooding. Long before an atoll is permanently under water, it may become impossible to live on. Storms and unusually high tides already push seawater across some islands, damaging homes and roads. Just as seriously, salt water seeps into the thin layer of fresh groundwater on which atoll communities depend for drinking and for growing crops. In Tuvalu, for example, the deep pits in which families have traditionally grown a type of giant taro have been badly affected by salt in some areas.

The leaders of atoll nations have used dramatic gestures to draw the world's attention to their situation. In 2009, the president of the Maldives, Mohamed Nasheed, held a cabinet meeting underwater, with ministers in diving equipment signing a call for cuts in global emissions. In 2021, Tuvalu's foreign minister, Simon Kofe, recorded a speech for an international climate conference while standing knee-deep in the sea. In my view, such images have been more effective than many years of technical reports in making distant governments understand what is at stake.

Some governments have begun to plan for the worst. In 2014, Kiribati bought a plot of land of around six thousand acres on Vanua Levu, one of the islands of Fiji. The government said it would be used mainly to grow food, but the then president, Anote Tong, also spoke of the possibility that his people might one day need to move there. Fiji itself has already relocated several coastal villages to higher ground, beginning in 2014 with the village of Vunidogoloa, and has identified dozens more communities that may need to move in the future.

Others have chosen to build. The Maldives has created an artificial island, Hulhumalé, near the capital, by pumping sand from the sea floor onto a shallow reef. Work began in 1997, and the new island stands about two metres above sea level, higher than most natural islands in the country. It is now home to tens of thousands of people. Critics point out, however, that such projects are expensive, can damage surrounding reefs, and are beyond the means of the poorest atoll states.

Science offers a more complicated picture than the headlines sometimes suggest. Coral islands are not fixed lumps of rock; they are made of sediment that is constantly moved by waves and currents, and new material is supplied by living reefs. A study published in 2018 by a team led by the geomorphologist Paul Kench found that the total land area of Tuvalu's 101 islands had actually increased slightly between 1971 and 2014, even though sea levels in the region had risen. Some islands had shrunk, but more had grown. I would argue that this finding is a reason for careful planning rather than for complacency, because it depends on healthy reefs, which are themselves threatened by warming oceans.

The situation also raises difficult legal questions. Under the Montevideo Convention of 1933, a state is generally understood to require a defined territory and a permanent population. What happens to a country if its people are forced to leave and its land disappears? Would it still have a seat at the United Nations, or control over the fishing grounds around its former islands, which are a vital source of income? In 2023, the leaders of the Pacific Islands Forum declared that the statehood of their members would continue regardless of the impact of sea-level rise, and Tuvalu has begun recording its land, culture and history in digital form.

In the same year, Tuvalu and Australia signed a treaty that allows up to two hundred and eighty Tuvaluans each year to move to Australia to live, work and study. Some welcomed this as a model of how wealthy countries could help, while others worried that it might encourage the slow emptying of the islands. It seems to me that the real test of the international community is not whether it offers new homes elsewhere, but whether it does enough to cut emissions so that people can choose to remain in the homes they already have.
